title: The Model Is Replaceable. The Learning Loop Is the Moat
body_text: Satya Nadella just gave enterprises one of the clearest mainstream signals yet: the model itself is no longer the thing to build around. That argument has been circulating for a while in AI circles, but hearing it framed this plainly matters. It reinforces a shift that many companies still have not fully internalized: the long-term advantage in enterprise AI is not the general-purpose model you plug in today. It is the system you build around your own workflows, your own data, and your own outcomes. The model is becoming a swappable input. The real moat is everything that happens around it. Why the model is no longer the moat For a while, many companies treated access to the most advanced frontier model as if it were the foundation of a defensible AI strategy. That made sense at an earlier stage of the market, when model capabilities were changing rapidly and access itself felt scarce. But that framing is becoming harder to defend. If a better generalist model appears tomorrow, your AI system should be able to adopt it without losing the intelligence your company has built up over time. In other words, the model should behave like a replaceable engine part, not the identity of the machine. A strong enterprise AI system should preserve what is uniquely yours even when the underlying model changes. If swapping one model for another breaks the value of your system, then much of the intelligence was never really yours to begin with. That is why the more useful analogy is not “which model won?” but “what did your company learn while using it?” Company-specific expertise is where the value compounds A frontier model may be powerful, but it does not automatically know how your business defines quality, what your internal edge cases look like, or how your teams make tradeoffs in practice. That expertise lives inside your organization. It shows up in the traces your users generate, the corrections they make, the judgments your best operators repeat, and the patterns your team gradually refines over time. This is the difference between a generalist and a company veteran. A generalist can be impressive across many contexts. A veteran understands how your organization actually works. The goal, then, is not to worship the generalist. The goal is to use the generalist to help encode, accelerate, and preserve the judgment of the company veteran. That means building systems that can absorb feedback from real use, learn from task-specific decisions, and improve against outcomes your organization actually cares about. Over time, this becomes institutional memory in operational form. Not just documents. Not just prompts. A living system that becomes sharper because your team keeps using it. That is the part that compounds. Private evals and private learning loops matter more than public benchmarks Public model benchmarks can tell you something about general capability, but they cannot tell you whether a system is actually getting better at your work. That is why private evaluation matters. The strongest AI organizations increasingly evaluate models against their own outcomes, not just public leaderboards. They measure performance on their own tasks, their own standards, and their own business-critical definitions of success. They do not outsource the question of quality to a benchmark designed for everyone else. From there, the next layer is even more important: the learning loop. When your system is evaluated on private outcomes and improved using private traces, you are creating a closed feedback loop that belongs to your company. Every usage cycle can make the system more aligned to your operating reality. Every correction can become signal. Every repeated workflow can become training for better performance tomorrow. That loop is more strategically important than the model currently sitting underneath it. Because once the loop is working, model upgrades become easier to absorb. You are no longer rebuilding from scratch every time the model market changes. You are carrying forward the part that matters most: your company’s accumulated learning. The “new IP of the firm” only compounds if you own it This is the strategic point many enterprises still underestimate. If your data, traces, and learning dynamics remain in infrastructure you do not control, then the compounding value may not stay with you. The insights generated by your workflows, the refinements produced by your operators, and the feedback that sharpens performance over time are only defensible if they remain inside a loop you own. Otherwise, you may be participating in someone else’s compounding curve. That is the risk behind treating AI as a rented advantage. From the outside, it can look like progress. Internally, teams may feel they are moving fast. But if the underlying learning does not stay attached to the enterprise, then differentiation does not deepen in proportion to usage. And that is when the illusion breaks. Two competitors can license the same model. Two competitors can use similar interfaces. Two competitors can adopt similar workflows. But the one that owns its evaluation loop, its traces, and its institutional learning will quietly become harder to copy over time. The one that does not may eventually discover that its “AI advantage” looks almost identical to everyone else’s. Conclusion The next cycle of enterprise AI will not be defined by who picked the right generalist model once. It will be defined by who built systems that keep learning in ways that are specific, private, and cumulative. The model is increasingly replaceable. The loop is not. The enterprises that understand this early will spend the next phase compounding their internal advantage. The ones that continue renting the core of their learning process may still adopt AI, but they will struggle to turn that adoption into something durable. That is the real shift behind Nadella’s message. The moat was never the weights. It was always the learning loop.

body_text: View All News BrilliA Incorporated Sponsors Celebrity Pickleball Tournament in Vietnam to Expand its Diana Brand Presence July 16, 2026 Download (opens in new window) Sponsorship highlights Diana brand as pickleball participation accelerates across Southeast Asia SINGAPORE--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- BrilliA Incorporated (NYSE American: BRIA) (“BrilliA” or the “Company”) today announced its sponsorship of a celebrity pickleball tournament hosted at the famous Ho Tram resort in Vietnam, showcasing its Diana footwear and apparel brand while expanding its presence in one of Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing sports market. The Mr & Miss Pickleball Vietnam 2026 tournament, held July 9-10, brought together competitive and recreational players from across the region and provided BrilliA with an opportunity to engage directly with Vietnam’s rapidly growing pickleball community. Pickleball continues to experience rapid growth throughout Asia, with Vietnam, Malaysia, and Singapore emerging as leading markets. Rising participation, increasing investment in dedicated courts, expanding tournament calendars and growing consumer interest have created attractive opportunities for brands focused on pickleball apparel, footwear and accessories. “Vietnam represents one of the most exciting pickleball markets in Southeast Asia, and we believe the sport is still in its early stages of long-term growth,” said Kendrew Hartanto, CEO of BrilliA. “Our sponsorship of this tournament reflects our strategy of building the Diana brand through direct engagement with players and the broader pickleball community. We see significant opportunities to expand our presence alongside the continued growth of the sport throughout the region.” The Mr & Miss Pickleball Vietnam 2026 tournament featured players from across Vietnam and neighbouring markets and included product displays and on-site brand activations highlighting Diana’s footwear and apparel collection. The sponsorship reflects BrilliA’s broader strategy of increasing brand awareness through participating in leading pickleball events across Southeast Asia. About the Diana Brand Diana has a product line dedicated to players who demand mobility, comfort, and style on the court. Built to support quick lateral movement, pivots, and sprints, Diana products combine lightweight, flexible construction with court-ready durability, allowing players to move freely without sacrificing fashion. The line is designed to appeal to the growing demographic of pickleball players seeking gear that performs as well as it looks, both on and off the court. Pickleball Market Opportunity Pickleball continues to gain momentum worldwide, with industry research estimating the global market for pickleball equipment, apparel and accessories at approximately $2 billion to $3 billion in 2025. Asia-Pacific is widely viewed as the fastest-growing region, with Vietnam, Malaysia and Singapore among the markets experiencing particularly strong growth in participation and court development. Based on publicly available industry research and Company estimates, BrilliA believes the market for pickleball apparel, footwear and accessories across these three countries represents a meaningful long-term growth opportunity for the Diana brand as participation and consumer spending continue to increase. Market information referenced above is based on third-party industry research and Company estimates and is provided for illustrative purposes only. About BrilliA Incorporated BrilliA Incorporated (NYSE American: BRIA) is a Singapore-based comprehensive one-stop service and solution provider for over 30 ladies’ intimate apparel brands worldwide, managing sourcing, design, prototyping, supply chain, logistics, and quality control. The Company works with major international companies, including Fruit of the Loom, HanesBrands Inc., and H&M. Through its Diana brand, BrilliA also designs and markets footwear and apparel for active lifestyles, including the rapidly growing sport of pickleball. Find out more at brilliaincorporated.com . title: Top AI Agent Use Cases for Sports Leagues
summary: AI Agent Use Cases for Sports Leagues: From the Field to the Front Office
body_text: The sports industry has always been defined by competition, the relentless pursuit of marginal gains, smarter strategy, and deeper fan connection. Today, that pursuit has a new engine: AI agents. Across professional leagues, franchises, and sports organizations worldwide, AI agents for sports are moving from pilot projects into production, reshaping how teams train, how fans experience games, and how front offices operate. The AI in sports market was valued at approximately $1 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $2.6 billion by 2030, a 16.7% annual growth rate that reflects just how seriously organizations are investing in this technology. And it's not hard to see why. When a single AI agent can compress three weeks of travel logistics planning into 20 minutes, or generate over 1,200 pieces of content per week at a fraction of the cost of human production, the operational argument becomes impossible to ignore. Here's a look at the most compelling use cases where AI agents are already making a measurable difference in sports. Player Performance Analysis and Injury Prevention Perhaps no use case carries more direct competitive stakes than player health and performance. Professional athletes experience an average of 62 injuries per 100 players per season, a number that carries enormous financial, strategic, and human costs. AI agents address this by continuously ingesting data from wearables, GPS trackers, heart rate monitors, and video feeds, then running predictive models in real time. When an athlete's sprint speed dips, their sleep patterns shift, or their workload spikes beyond a defined threshold, the agent surfaces an alert to the medical or coaching staff, before a small problem becomes a season-ending injury. This isn't just about flagging risk. Agents also generate personalized training recommendations, adjusting intensity, recovery windows, and drill selection based on each athlete's current physical state and historical patterns. The result is a feedback loop that's faster, more consistent, and more objective than any human analyst could sustain across an entire squad. The NFL has deployed systems of this kind through its Digital Athlete program, running millions of game simulations to identify which players face the highest injury risk on any given week. Teams use those predictions to design individualized prevention and recovery programs, a workflow that simply wasn't possible at scale before agentic AI. Intelligent Scouting and Talent Identification Traditional scouting is expensive, time-intensive, and inherently subjective. Sending human scouts to cover regional leagues across multiple countries requires significant resources, and the insights they return are limited by what any individual can observe and remember. AI agents are fundamentally changing that equation. By processing video footage from local and regional leagues, agents can automatically identify players with standout movement patterns, decision-making speed, and technical execution, building detailed profiles without a single plane ticket. Organizations that have adopted AI-assisted scouting report reductions in scouting hours of up to 70%, while simultaneously improving the breadth and consistency of talent evaluation. Beyond raw identification, agents can compare prospects against historical player benchmarks, flag comparable profiles from past drafts, and even model how a player might fit within a specific team's tactical system. The output isn't a gut feeling, it's a layered, data-backed view of a prospect's long-term value. This capability is particularly valuable for smaller clubs that historically couldn't compete with the scouting networks of larger organizations. AI agents are leveling the playing field, making elite-level talent intelligence accessible to teams at every budget tier. Real-Time Game Strategy and Coaching Support In-game decision-making has always been one of the highest-pressure environments in sports. Coaches have minutes, sometimes seconds, to process what they're seeing and respond. AI agents are now acting as a real-time intelligence layer that augments those decisions. On NFL sidelines, coaches equipped with AI-enabled tablets receive automatically filtered footage of relevant plays based on live game conditions, down, distance, field position, without manually searching through footage. The agent surfaces what's most relevant, when it's most needed. At halftime, agents can analyze the first half's data and generate tactical recommendations: which formations are creating openings, where the opposing defense is showing vulnerability, which substitutions would improve the team's probability of winning. These aren't static reports, they're dynamic recommendations that adapt as the game evolves. The Oakland Ballers recently became the first professional baseball team to have AI support most game management decisions, including setting lineups and managing in-game substitutions. The experiment revealed something important: AI can process data faster and more effectively than humans in many situations, but emotional leadership, motivation, and situational nuance still require a human touch. The most effective deployments treat AI agents as collaborators, not replacements. Automated Content Creation and Media Production Sports media operates on an impossible timeline. Games end, and fans immediately want recaps, highlights, analysis, and commentary, across websites, social media, apps, and broadcast platforms simultaneously. For most organizations, human editorial teams simply can't keep up with demand at scale. AI agents are solving this through multi-agent content workflows. One prominent example involves a major golf organization that deployed a network of specialized agents, research agents, writer agents, validation agents, and editor agents, to generate over 1,200 pieces of content per week, at less than 25 cents per piece. That represents a 95% cost reduction compared to previous vendor-dependent processes. The system generates round recaps, tournament summaries, player betting profiles, and shot-by-shot commentary for all 150+ players in a tournament field, content types that were previously impossible to produce at that scale. Crucially, validation agents check every factual claim against live data before publication, ensuring accuracy alongside speed. Beyond text, AI agents are also automating highlight generation. Systems can detect key moments, a goal, a slam dunk, a record-breaking serve, the instant they occur, clip them automatically, and push personalized highlight reels to fans within minutes of the event. A fan who wants every three-pointer from their favorite player, assembled and delivered to their phone before they go to sleep, can now have exactly that. Personalized Fan Engagement The fan relationship has always been the commercial foundation of sports. But for most of history, that relationship was one-to-many: the same broadcast, the same email, the same in-stadium experience for everyone. AI agents make it genuinely one-to-one. By connecting CRM data with behavioral signals, what content fans engage with, which seats they prefer, what food they order, which players they follow, agents can deliver experiences that feel tailored to each individual. One MLS club built an agentic tool that integrates with ticketing, concessions, retail, and league statistics systems, allowing fans to ask natural language questions and receive real-time, personalized answers on matchday. The system can recommend nearby concessions based on a fan's seating location and past preferences, surface real-time stadium policy information during weather delays, and guide the overall matchday experience. Other franchises are using AI agents to send personalized emails that adapt content, tone, and even visual styling to individual fan behavior. Dynamic marketing systems trigger in-the-moment offers based on real-time signals, a fan who just watched a player's highlight reel might receive a jersey offer minutes later. Research suggests roughly one in four sports fans would pay more for personalized, AI-enhanced experiences, a direct commercial path to increased revenue per fan and stronger long-term loyalty. Operations and Logistics Automation Behind every game-day experience is an enormous operational apparatus: travel logistics, scheduling, vendor coordination, staffing, and compliance. Much of this work is repetitive, high-volume, and prone to human error, exactly the kind of work AI agents handle well. One NBA franchise reduced its full season travel logistics planning from three weeks to 20 minutes using AI. Agents handle the complex constraint satisfaction problem of coordinating flights, hotels, and ground transportation across an 82-game season, factoring in rest requirements, back-to-back games, and arena availability. In sponsorship and commercial operations, AI agents are automating the matching of athletes with brand partners, turning campaigns that once took days of negotiation and research into near-instant recommendations. Agents analyze an athlete's audience demographics, engagement rates, and brand alignment to surface the most relevant partnership opportunities, and can draft initial outreach materials automatically. For sports organizations managing large venues, AI agents are also being deployed to handle work orders, vendor communications, and facility management workflows, reducing response times and freeing operations staff to focus on higher-value problem-solving. Officiating Support and Game Integrity Officiating has always been one of the most contested aspects of sports. Human referees operate under extreme time pressure, with limited viewing angles and the inherent fallibility of perception. AI agents are increasingly acting as a support layer that improves accuracy without removing human judgment from the equation. In tennis, image recognition systems help line judges detect whether balls land in or out with a level of precision that eliminates controversy. In soccer, AI-powered cameras deliver real-time verdicts on goal validity, offside calls, and potential fouls, augmenting what the on-field officials can see. These systems are designed to work alongside human officials, not replace them. The goal is to reduce the frequency of consequential errors, not to automate the entire officiating process. As the technology matures, the same systems used at elite levels are becoming accessible to lower divisions and youth leagues, raising the standard of officiating across the entire sport. Bringing It All Together: The Enterprise Opportunity What makes AI agents particularly powerful in sports is that these use cases don't operate in isolation. A well-designed agentic system can connect player performance data to content generation, feed injury predictions into scheduling decisions, and link fan behavior signals to commercial activations, all within a single, governed workflow. The organizations seeing the greatest returns aren't treating AI as a collection of point solutions. They're building integrated intelligence layers that connect their existing systems, CRM, ticketing, video platforms, wearables, scheduling tools, and deploying agents that can reason across all of that data to produce outcomes no single tool could achieve alone. That integration-first approach is what separates organizations that are genuinely transforming their operations from those still running disconnected experiments. The teams moving fastest are the ones treating AI agents not as a technology novelty, but as a core operational capability, one that compounds in value as more data flows through it and more workflows connect to it. For sports organizations ready to build that kind of capability, the conversation starts with understanding what's possible and mapping it to the specific workflows where the impact will be greatest. title: How to Advise Students on Industries Outside Your Experience
summary: A practical guide for higher-ed career advisors who coach students into industries they have never worked in. Learn what to track, which sources to trust, how to build shared industry knowledge, and when to involve employers, alumni, faculty, or specialists.
body_text: How can career advisors advise students on industries outside their experience? Career advisors can advise students on industries outside their experience by focusing on role structure, employer evidence, recruiting timelines, selection formats, credentials, and market changes that affect student decisions. Advisors do not need to know every technical detail of a field, but they should know how to verify current information, compare sources, ask evidence-based questions, and identify when a student needs deeper industry expertise. A strong advising model uses occupational data, current job postings, primary industry sources, employers, alumni, and faculty to keep guidance current. The goal is to help students interpret roles, prepare evidence, and make informed decisions without guessing or overstating uncertain information. If you advise students across multiple industries, you will eventually face questions about fields you have never worked in yourself. A student may ask about software engineering interviews, finance recruiting timelines, healthcare credentials, technical portfolios, or specialized roles, and expect a clear answer during the appointment. The challenge is knowing what guidance you can provide confidently, what information needs to be checked, and when the student would benefit from someone with deeper industry expertise. This guide provides a practical way to handle those situations. It explains which industry information advisors should keep current, where to verify it, how career teams can divide responsibility for different fields, and how to continue helping students without guessing or presenting uncertain information as fact. Why Does Advising Outside Your Industry Experience Feel Difficult? Advising an unfamiliar industry is difficult because students may expect answers that combine career coaching, current hiring knowledge, technical fluency, and insider experience. The advisor may understand decision-making and job-search strategy while lacking direct knowledge of how work or recruitment operates in that specific field. The credibility gap usually appears in questions such as: Which technical skills are employers prioritizing right now? Does this portfolio demonstrate enough depth? How early does recruiting begin? Is this certification expected or simply helpful? How different are roles with similar titles? What does an entry-level interview actually test? Is the student interpreting the industry accurately? These questions should not force an advisor into one of two weak positions: giving confident but unverified answers or becoming so cautious that the student receives no usable guidance. The advisor knows which parts of the conversation can be coached directly, which information needs current verification, and which questions require someone closer to the field. What Does an Advisor Actually Need to Know About an Industry? An advisor does not need to perform the job or understand every technical detail. They only need enough industry literacy to help the student interpret roles, evaluate evidence, prepare appropriately, and recognize when general career advice no longer applies. The advisor should understand The advisor does not need to master Major role families and how they differ Every job title used across the industry Common entry routes and recruiting timelines The complete internal hiring process of every employer Skills, experiences, and credentials that repeatedly appear in current roles How to personally perform each technical task Typical application and interview formats How to score advanced technical work without a suitable rubric Differences between required, preferred, and employer-specific qualifications Every certification or licensing exception Important work conditions, such as client interaction, shifts, travel, regulation, or project cycles The daily workflow of every occupation Where reliable information can be verified A definitive answer to every student question When to involve an industry specialist, faculty member, employer, or alum Becoming the permanent expert for the field Students rarely need an advisor to explain the technical work itself, such as how to build a software system, value a financial instrument, or deliver clinical care. What they do need is help understanding which roles fit their interests , whether their experience demonstrates the skills employers expect, and what additional information they need before choosing a direction. Which Industry Information Should Advisors Keep Current? Advisors should monitor the parts of an industry that directly change student decisions and preparation. General news about mergers, stock prices, or prominent companies may be interesting, but it rarely improves an advising appointment unless it affects entry-level roles or hiring. Focus on six categories. 1. Entry-Level Role Structure Track the main functions available to students rather than memorizing hundreds of titles. For example, “technology” may include software development, data analysis, cybersecurity, product management, technical consulting, quality assurance, implementation, customer success, and technology operations. The first advising task is often helping the student identify which function they mean. 2. Evidence Employers Request Look for the evidence that repeatedly appears across current opportunities: Projects Internships or clinical experience Portfolios Research Certifications Coursework Leadership Customer-facing experience Technical tools Writing or presentation samples The advisor should distinguish between a capability employers want and the evidence recruiters expect students to provide . 3. Recruiting Timing Some industries recruit far earlier than students expect. Others hire closer to need. Advisors should know whether the field commonly uses structured annual cycles, rolling recruitment, cohort programs, residency or fellowship deadlines, or employer-specific schedules. The objective is not to remember every deadline. It is to recognize when the student needs to begin checking current timelines immediately. 4. Selection Formats Track how employers commonly assess early-career candidates. Depending on the field, that may include: Technical assessments Coding interviews Case interviews Portfolio presentations Financial modelling tests Recorded interviews Clinical experience discussions Research presentations Assessment centers Multiple behavioral interview rounds Recognizing these formats helps the advisor direct students toward the right preparation method. Advanced technical responses may still require evaluation from someone with field-specific expertise. 5. Credentials and Constraints Advisors should understand when a credential appears to be: Legally or professionally required Commonly preferred Relevant only to certain functions Employer-sponsored after hiring Helpful but not worth delaying applications for Dependent on location, setting, or role level Healthcare is an obvious example because clinical, public-health, research, health-technology, pharmaceutical, and healthcare-administration roles can have substantially different requirements. 6. Changes That Affect Early-Career Candidates A market development becomes advising-relevant when it changes what students should research, demonstrate, practice, or expect. Useful questions include: Are employers adding a new skill to entry-level postings? Are interview formats changing? Are employers consolidating previously separate roles? Is a tool becoming common enough to influence student preparation? Are internship requirements appearing more frequently? Are certain credentials losing or gaining relevance? Are recruiting timelines moving? This keeps the advisor focused on student implications rather than trying to follow every industry headline. Which Sources Should Advisors Use to Stay Current? Advisors should combine structured occupational data, current hiring evidence, primary industry sources, and direct field validation. No single source can explain an entire industry accurately. Start with the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook , which organizes occupations into groups including computer and information technology, business and financial, and healthcare. It allows you to compare education, training, pay, projected openings, and growth across occupations. Use O*NET OnLine when the advisor needs more detail about tasks, knowledge, abilities, work activities, career clusters, industries, and technologies associated with an occupation. It covers more than 900 occupations and includes software skills frequently mentioned in employer postings. Use a Small Sample of Current Job Postings A structured review of current job descriptions across ten to fifteen relevant internships and entry-level roles can reveal: Repeated skills and tools Variations in job titles Required versus preferred qualifications Evidence employers request Geographic differences Common responsibilities Application materials Experience expectations Do not turn one posting into a universal rule. One employer may have an unusual structure or inflated qualification list. The useful signals are the patterns repeated across different organizations. Prioritize Primary Industry Sources For rapidly changing or regulated fields, follow the organizations closest to the information. Depending on the industry, this could include: Professional associations Licensing or regulatory bodies Government agencies Accreditation organizations Major employer early-career pages Industry research institutes Official workforce reports Employer engineering, research, or clinical publications Newsletters and social media can surface a development, but advisors should verify the underlying claim before adding it to student guidance. Maintain a Clear Source Hierarchy Use occupational data to understand the field broadly, postings to understand current hiring language, primary industry sources to investigate changes, and practitioners to verify how those changes appear in actual work. This reduces the risk of giving students advice based on one viral post, one alum’s experience, or one unusually selective employer. How Can Advisors Build an Industry-Update Routine That Fits Their Workload? Industry awareness should be maintained through a small recurring routine rather than occasional deep research. The objective is to notice decision-relevant changes and keep shared advising guidance dated and verifiable. Cadence Advisor activity Practical output Weekly Record unfamiliar questions, new job titles, employer comments, and student misconceptions that surfaced in appointments A short list of items requiring verification Monthly Review a small posting sample and one or two primary sources for the assigned industry cluster Updated notes on roles, skills, credentials, or recruiting Quarterly Validate the main changes with an employer-relations colleague, faculty member, alum, recruiter, or practitioner Confirmed guidance and corrected assumptions Each semester Review student-facing guides, workshop examples, interview preparation, referral contacts, and outdated claims A refreshed industry briefing for the advising team A monthly scan should not become an attempt to read the entire industry. It can follow five steps: Select two or three common early-career functions. Review current postings from several employers. note repeated changes in qualifications, tools, or selection methods. Verify important changes through a primary source or practitioner. Update the shared industry briefing with a date and source. The Duke University Data & Technology Career Community demonstrates the value of organizing a changing field through a curated collection of industry insights, professional associations, technical-interview guidance, jobs, internships, courses, and advisor access. Career centers do not need every advisor independently rebuilding that information from scratch. How Should Career Centers Divide Industry Coverage? Career centers should divide coverage into broad, manageable clusters and give each cluster a clear owner. Asking every generalist to stay current on every industry creates duplication while still leaving important areas unattended. Possible clusters include: Data, technology, and engineering Business, finance, and consulting Healthcare and life sciences Government, policy, and social impact Education and human services Arts, media, and communications Environment, energy, and sustainability Ownership does not mean one advisor must handle every student interested in that field. The owner maintains the briefing, monitors common questions, coordinates verification, and alerts the team when guidance changes. The University of Florida Career Connections Center uses career clusters that group occupations and industries with related knowledge and skills. Its Career Communities are organized around industry and affinity groupings rather than being attached exclusively to academic majors. Career teams can adapt the same logic internally by assigning advisors to monitor a cluster instead of individual occupations. An industry briefing can remain concise. Include: Main entry-level functions Common student misconceptions Typical experience signals Recruiting calendar Common selection formats Relevant credentials Work-context considerations Reliable sources Internal and external referral contacts Date last reviewed How Can Employers, Alumni, and Faculty Strengthen Advisor Knowledge? Structured employer partnerships , combined with alumni and faculty expertise, can form an advisor-verification network for questions that public sources cannot answer clearly. Instead of requesting a general industry presentation, ask narrow questions: Which entry-level roles are students confusing with one another? Which qualifications are frequently listed but not decisive? What evidence helps a student demonstrate readiness? Which interview stage produces the most avoidable failures? Which advice given to students is now outdated? What has changed in your function during the past year? Which questions should a generalist advisor refer to rather than answer? Narrow questions produce information that can be turned into advising guidance. A broad “tell us about your industry” discussion often produces personal career stories without clarifying how the team should coach students. The Rutgers Healthcare and Life Sciences Career Community shows one way to distribute expertise. Career advisors work alongside industry connectors, industry consultants who are recruiters, other specialists, alumni mentors, and a community advisory board. This allows the advisor to remain part of the student’s support system without serving as the only source of industry knowledge. What Should Advisors Say When They Do Not Know the Answer? Advisors can protect credibility by being precise about what they know, what needs verification, and how the student can move forward. Acknowledging an information gap is more useful than offering a confident generalization. Use language such as: When the question is employer-specific “I can help you prepare for the decision, but I do not want to assume this employer uses the same process as others in the field. Let’s verify its current requirements and interview stages.” When the student presents one source as an industry rule “That may be accurate for this organization. Before treating it as an industry expectation, let’s check whether it appears across several comparable roles.” When a credential may not be universally required “This credential appears relevant to some roles, but its value may depend on the function, employer, and location. Let’s verify where it is required, preferred, or optional.” When technical evaluation exceeds the advisor’s role “I can review whether the project communicates scope, contribution, and outcomes clearly. A technical reviewer should assess the depth of the implementation.” When the field is changing “The guidance on this issue appears to be changing. I can help you identify the current evidence, compare sources, and decide what preparation is sensible now.” These responses keep the appointment moving. The advisor is still helping the student evaluate information, ask better questions, and identify a next step. Which Questions Can Generalist Advisors Still Ask Confidently? Strong advising questions remain useful across industries because they help the student examine evidence rather than depend on the advisor for insider answers. Ask: Which functions within this industry are you actually considering? What patterns appear across the roles you have reviewed? Which qualifications are consistently required? What evidence do you currently have for the skills employers request? Which expectations are based on several sources, and which came from one person? What part of the selection process are you least prepared for? What would you need to learn from someone working in the field? Which constraint matters most: training time, location, cost, schedule, compensation, or work environment? What information is still missing before you make this decision? These questions reposition the advisor from industry lecturer to decision facilitator. They also reveal when the student has done meaningful research and when assumptions are driving the conversation. When Should a Generalist Advisor Refer a Student? Referral is appropriate when the student’s question requires specialized judgment, regulated guidance, employer-specific knowledge, or technical evaluation that cannot be supported reliably through the advisor’s current sources. Refer or consult when: Licensure, accreditation, or professional eligibility affects the student’s options A technical student portfolio , coding project, financial model, research sample, or clinical experience needs field-level evaluation. The student is entering an unusually specialized recruiting process Employer-specific practices cannot be confirmed publicly A decision carries substantial academic, financial, immigration, or professional consequences Current sources conflict The advisor would otherwise need to speculate The student needs access to a professional who can explain the lived reality of the work A referral should not end with “talk to an alum.” Give the student a specific purpose and set of questions. For example: “Speak with someone who entered healthcare consulting within the past three years. Ask which experiences helped them demonstrate both analytical ability and familiarity with healthcare settings, and which qualifications employers actually examined during recruitment.” The clearer the research task, the more likely the student is to return with useful information. How Can Career Centers Keep Industry Knowledge From Living in One Person’s Head? Career centers need shared operating procedures for capturing industry knowledge so it survives staff transitions and remains consistent across appointments. Otherwise, the advisor who happens to follow finance, technology, or healthcare becomes the informal help desk for the entire office. Use one shared location for: Industry briefings Source links Frequently asked student questions Verified employer insights Recruiting-cycle notes Common interview formats Referral contacts Recent changes Items still requiring confirmation Review dates and owners Team meetings can include a five-minute “market change” item in which one advisor shares a verified change and explains how it affects student guidance. The update should answer three questions: What changed? Which students or appointments are affected? What should advisors say or do differently? Converting every industry development into a new policy is not really required. Many updates require only a corrected example, an added question, a revised referral, or a note that the team should avoid making an absolute claim. Wrapping Up Advisors do not need direct experience in every industry to provide credible guidance. They need reliable sources, current hiring evidence, a structured way to capture what they learn, and clear referral points for questions requiring deeper technical or professional expertise. Hiration helps students handle more career preparation across exploration, resumes, cover letters, LinkedIn, interviews, and job search. Its Counselor Module gives career teams visibility into assignments, progress, feedback, and students who need additional support within a FERPA- and SOC 2-compliant platform. This gives advisors more time to interpret industry information and guide decisions that require human judgment. Book a walkthrough to see how Hiration can support advising across different industries. Advising Students on Unfamiliar Industries — FAQs How can career advisors advise students on industries outside their experience? Career advisors can help students by focusing on transferable advising work: clarifying the student’s target function, identifying current employer expectations, checking reliable sources, comparing evidence, preparing questions, and referring the student when technical or regulated expertise is needed. Why does advising outside your industry experience feel difficult? It feels difficult because students may ask questions that combine career coaching, current hiring knowledge, technical fluency, recruiting timelines, portfolio standards, credentials, and insider experience. Advisors may understand job-search strategy while still needing current verification for field-specific details. What does an advisor actually need to know about an industry? Advisors need enough industry literacy to help students interpret roles, evaluate whether their evidence matches employer expectations, prepare for common selection formats, understand timing, and recognize when general career advice no longer applies. They do not need to perform the technical work themselves. Which industry information should advisors keep current? Advisors should keep current on entry-level role structures, evidence employers request, recruiting timelines, selection formats, required or preferred credentials, and changes that affect early-career candidates. These categories are more useful in advising than general industry headlines. Why should advisors track entry-level role structure? Entry-level role structure helps advisors clarify what the student actually means by an industry. For example, technology may include software development, data analysis, cybersecurity, product management, consulting, quality assurance, implementation, customer success, and operations. What employer evidence should advisors help students identify? Advisors should help students identify evidence employers repeatedly request, such as projects, internships, clinical experience, portfolios, research, certifications, coursework, leadership, technical tools, customer-facing experience, writing samples, or presentation samples. Why do recruiting timelines matter in unfamiliar industries? Recruiting timelines matter because some industries recruit much earlier than students expect, while others hire closer to need. Advisors should recognize whether a field uses structured annual cycles, rolling recruitment, fellowship deadlines, residency timelines, or employer-specific schedules. Which selection formats should advisors monitor? Advisors should monitor selection formats such as technical assessments, coding interviews, case interviews, portfolio presentations, financial modeling tests, recorded interviews, clinical experience discussions, research presentations, assessment centers, and multiple behavioral interview rounds. How should advisors think about credentials and certifications? Advisors should distinguish whether a credential is legally required, commonly preferred, relevant only to certain functions, employer-sponsored after hiring, helpful but optional, or dependent on location, setting, or role level. Students should not delay applications for credentials without verifying their actual value. Which sources should advisors use to stay current? Advisors should combine occupational data, current job postings, primary industry sources, professional associations, licensing or regulatory bodies, employer early-career pages, official workforce reports, alumni, employers, and faculty. No single source can explain an industry accurately. How should advisors use job postings for industry research? Advisors should review a small sample of current postings across comparable internships or entry-level roles to identify repeated skills, tools, job titles, qualifications, responsibilities, application materials, and experience expectations. One posting should not be treated as an industry rule. What is a useful source hierarchy for industry advising? A useful hierarchy is to use occupational data for broad field structure, current postings for hiring language, primary industry sources for changing requirements, and practitioners for validation. This reduces reliance on one viral post, one alum’s experience, or one unusually selective employer. How can advisors build an industry-update routine? Advisors can use a small monthly routine: select two or three common early-career functions, review current postings, note repeated changes in qualifications or selection methods, verify important changes through a primary source or practitioner, and update a shared briefing with the date and source. How should career centers divide industry coverage? Career centers can divide coverage into broad clusters such as technology and engineering, business and finance, healthcare and life sciences, government and social impact, education and human services, arts and communications, or environment and sustainability. Each cluster should have a clear owner. What should an industry briefing include? An industry briefing should include main entry-level functions, common student misconceptions, typical experience signals, recruiting calendar, common selection formats, relevant credentials, work-context considerations, reliable sources, referral contacts, and the date last reviewed. How can employers, alumni, and faculty strengthen advisor knowledge? Employers, alumni, and faculty can help advisors verify field-specific questions that public sources do not answer clearly. Career centers should ask narrow questions about role confusion, required evidence, outdated advice, interview stages, qualification signals, and what has changed in the field. What should advisors say when they do not know the answer? Advisors should be direct about what they know and what needs verification. They can say, “I can help you prepare for the decision, but I do not want to assume this employer uses the same process as others. Let’s verify the current requirements and interview stages.” Which questions can advisors still ask confidently across industries? Advisors can ask which functions the student is considering, what patterns appear across roles, which qualifications are consistently required, what evidence the student has, which expectations came from several sources, what selection stage feels least prepared, and what information is still missing. When should advisors refer a student to someone with deeper expertise? Referral is appropriate when the question involves licensure, accreditation, technical portfolio evaluation, specialized recruiting, employer-specific practices, conflicting sources, immigration or financial consequences, or any situation where the advisor would otherwise need to speculate. How can career centers preserve industry knowledge across the team? Career centers should store industry briefings, source links, student questions, employer insights, recruiting notes, interview formats, referral contacts, recent changes, unresolved questions, review dates, and owners in one shared location so knowledge does not remain in one advisor’s head. How can Hiration support advising across unfamiliar industries? Hiration can help students complete more preparation across career exploration, resumes, cover letters, LinkedIn, interviews, and job search before meeting with an advisor. Its Counselor Module gives career teams visibility into assignments, progress, feedback, and students who need additional support. summary: Prepárate para la temporada navideña con esta guía paso a paso. Optimiza tu tienda en línea, inventario y campañas para maximizar tus ventas en Navidad.
body_text: La temporada navideña es una de las épocas más importantes para el comercio electrónico. Para aprovechar al máximo esta oportunidad, es crucial que tu tienda en línea esté optimizada y lista para enfrentar el aumento de la demanda. Aquí te presentamos una guía paso a paso para preparar tu tienda y maximizar tus ventas durante la temporada navideña. 1. Optimiza tu inventario Antes de que la temporada comience, revisa tus productos y asegúrate de tener suficiente inventario para satisfacer la demanda navideña. Analiza los productos más vendidos de años anteriores y asegúrate de que los productos clave estén bien abastecidos. También es una buena idea introducir productos especiales o ediciones limitadas para las fiestas. Consejo: Usa herramientas de análisis de ventas para prever la demanda de productos y asegúrate de contar con suficiente stock sin sobrecargar tu inventario. 2. Mejora la experiencia de usuario en tu sitio Durante la época navideña, muchos compradores estarán explorando tu tienda por primera vez. Asegúrate de que tu sitio sea fácil de navegar y que la experiencia de compra sea fluida. Revisa que las páginas de producto carguen rápido, los botones de compra sean visibles y el proceso de checkout sea sencillo. Una buena experiencia de usuario puede ser la diferencia entre una venta y un carrito abandonado. Tip adicional: Optimiza tu tienda para dispositivos móviles, ya que muchas compras navideñas se realizan desde smartphones. 3. Crea ofertas especiales y promociones Los compradores navideños buscan las mejores ofertas. Crea descuentos, promociones y combos atractivos para captar su atención. Considera ofrecer envío gratuito, descuentos por compras mínimas o promociones por tiempo limitado para generar un sentido de urgencia. Consejo: Planifica bien tus campañas promocionales en fechas clave, como el Buen Fin, Black Friday y las semanas previas a Navidad. 4. Optimiza el SEO de tu tienda para búsquedas navideñas Incorpora palabras clave relacionadas con la temporada navideña en los títulos, descripciones y metadatos de tus productos. Términos como “regalos de Navidad”, “ofertas navideñas” y “descuento especial” te ayudarán a aparecer en las búsquedas de los compradores que buscan regalos para las fiestas. Prepara tus campañas de marketing digital Mercado Libre ofrece una solución logística llamada Mercado Envíos que Tu estrategia de marketing digital es crucial para atraer tráfico a tu tienda durante la temporada navideña. Asegúrate de tener listas tus campañas de publicidad pagada en Google, redes sociales y marketplaces. Utiliza anuncios que destaquen tus promociones, productos estrella y envíos rápidos. Consejo: Segmenta tus campañas para llegar a audiencias específicas, como compradores recurrentes o aquellos interesados en productos similares a los que ofreces. 6. Refuerza la atención al cliente La temporada navideña puede generar un aumento en las preguntas y solicitudes de los clientes. Asegúrate de que tu equipo de atención al cliente esté preparado para responder rápidamente a cualquier duda o problema. Un servicio al cliente eficiente no solo ayuda a cerrar ventas, sino que también mejora la reputación de tu marca. Tip adicional: Considera automatizar parte de tu atención al cliente con chatbots que puedan responder preguntas frecuentes de manera inmediata. 7. Prepara tu logística y envíos La velocidad de los envíos es crítica durante la temporada navideña. Revisa tus acuerdos con los proveedores de logística y asegúrate de que puedan manejar el aumento de pedidos. Además, ofrece opciones de envío rápido para los compradores de última hora. Consumer Loan Marketplace Volume: We define Consumer Loan Marketplace Volume as the total U.S. dollar equivalent value of originations of HELOCs, DSCRs, and personal loans on our LOS, as well as the volume of third-party loans traded on Figure Connect. We believe this measure is an indication of our scale and represents the potential revenue opportunity from the technology used for consumer credit loan originations. $YLDS in Circulation: We define $YLDS in Circulation as the total U.S. dollar equivalent value of unsecured face-amount certificates solely backed by the assets of Figure Certificate Company (FCC), which is the issuer of the certificates. This is reported as an end of period outstanding balance. Matched Offers: We define Matched Offers as the U.S. dollar equivalent value of offers matched between borrowers and lenders on the Democratized Prime platform. This is reported as an end of period outstanding balance. Borrower Demand: We define Borrower Demand as the U.S. dollar equivalent value that borrowers seek to borrow from the lending pool on the Democratized Prime platform. This is reported as an end of period outstanding balance. Available Lender Supply: We define Lender Supply as the U.S. dollar equivalent value that lenders have made available in the lending pool on the Democratized Prime platform. This is reported as an end of period outstanding balance. More than 380 partners use its loan origination system and capital marketplace. Collectively, Figure and its partners have originated approximately $29 billion of home equity to date, among other products, making Figure’s ecosystem the largest non-bank provider of HELOCs. The fastest growing components are Figure Connect, its consumer credit marketplace, and Democratized Prime, Figure’s on-chain lend-borrow marketplace. Figure's ecosystem also includes DART (Digital Asset Registry Technology) for asset custody and lien perfection, and $YLDS, an SEC-registered yield-bearing stablecoin that operates as a tokenized money market fund. Figure is the market leader in real world asset (RWA) tokenization. body_text: View All News Atmus Filtration Technologies Completes Acquisition of Koch Filter Corporation January 7, 2026 NASHVILLE, Tenn.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Atmus Filtration Technologies Inc. (“Atmus”; NYSE: ATMU), a global leader in filtration and media solutions, today announced that it has closed its acquisition of Koch Filter Corporation (“Koch Filter”) from Air Distribution Technologies, Inc. (“ADTi”), a portfolio company of Truelink Capital, for a total cash consideration of approximately $450 million, subject to customary purchase price adjustments. The completion of the Koch Filter acquisition establishes Atmus’ industrial air filtration platform and expands its portfolio into high-growth end-markets, including commercial and industrial HVAC, data centers and power generation markets. “We are excited to welcome the Koch Filter team to Atmus. Together, we are committed to unlocking our growth potential and executing our strategy of expanding into industrial filtration markets,” said Steph Disher, Chief Executive Officer of Atmus. The acquisition establishes the Company’s new Industrial Solutions segment. The Koch Filter business will report into that segment and be led by Rakesh Gangwani, Senior Vice President, Strategy and President, Industrial Solutions. Mark Mattingly, Koch Filter’s president, who has deep industry experience established over three decades, will continue to lead the Koch Filter business, reporting to Rakesh Gangwani. Simultaneously with the closing of the transaction, Atmus entered an amended and restated five-year $1.5 billion credit facility, consisting of a $500 million revolving credit facility and a $1 billion term loan. As previously disclosed, the acquisition of Koch Filter is expected to be accretive to Atmus’ Adjusted EPS and Adjusted EBITDA margin in 2026 and achieve high-single-digit ROIC by 2028. The transaction was funded through a combination of cash on hand and borrowings under the Company’s amended and restated credit facility. About Atmus Filtration Technologies Inc. Atmus Filtration Technologies Inc. is a global leader in filtration and media solutions. For more than 65 years, the company has combined its culture of innovation with a rich history of designing and manufacturing filtration solutions. With a global presence spanning six continents, Atmus serves customers across truck, bus, agriculture, construction, mining, marine and power generation vehicle and equipment markets, along with providing comprehensive aftermarket support and solutions. Headquartered in Nashville, Tennessee (U.S.), Atmus employs approximately 4,500 people globally who are committed to creating a better future by protecting what is important. Learn more at https://www.atmus.com . Use of Non-GAAP Information We refer to certain non-GAAP financial measures in this press release, including Atmus’ Adjusted EPS and Adjusted EBITDA margin. These non-GAAP financial measures should not be considered alternatives to, or more meaningful indicators of, Atmus’ financial measures as prepared in accordance with GAAP. Atmus’ methods of determining these non-GAAP financial measures may differ from the methods used by other companies and may not be comparable. title: Genmab and AbbVie Provide Clarification on Phase 3 EPCORE® DLBCL-1 Trial Evaluating Epcoritamab (DuoBody®-CD3xCD20) in Patients with Relapsed/Refractory Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)
summary: Media Release COPENHAGEN, Denmark and NORTH CHICAGO, Ill.; July 23, 2026 Genmab and AbbVie clarify overall survival (OS) was the sole U.S. primary endpoint in the Phase 3 EPCORE ® DLBCL-1 trial and was not met Genmab A/S (Nasdaq: GMAB) and AbbVie (NYSE: ABBV) today provided clarification on the
body_text: Media Release COPENHAGEN, Denmark and NORTH CHICAGO, Ill.; July 23, 2026 Genmab and AbbVie clarify overall survival (OS) was the sole U.S. primary endpoint in the Phase 3 EPCORE ® DLBCL-1 trial and was not met Genmab A/S (Nasdaq: GMAB) and AbbVie (NYSE: ABBV) today provided clarification on the primary endpoints from the Phase 3 EPCORE ® DLBCL-1 study evaluating monotherapy epcoritamab (DuoBody®-CD3xCD20) , a T-cell engaging bispecific antibody administered subcutaneously, compared with investigator's choice of chemoimmunotherapy (CIT) of either rituximab plus gemcitabine plus oxaliplatin (R-GemOx) or bendamustine plus rituximab (BR) in adults with relapsed or refractory (R/R) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) who were ineligible for autologous stem cell transplantation. Genmab and AbbVie previously announced topline results of the study on January 16, 2026, and additional study results were subsequently presented at the European Hematology Association (EHA) 2026 Congress on June 12, 2026. EPCORE DLBCL-1 is a global, Phase 3, open label, multi-center, randomized clinical trial with prespecified primary endpoints that differ by region. In the United States, where overall survival (OS) is the sole primary endpoint, the study did not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in OS and therefore did not meet its primary endpoint. Additional results of the EPCORE DLBCL-1 study will be submitted for publication in a peer-reviewed medical journal. About Epcoritamab Epcoritamab is approved under the FDA's accelerated approval pathway for the treatment of adult patients with R/R DLBCL, not otherwise specified (NOS), including DLBCL arising from indolent lymphoma, and high-grade B-cell lymphoma, after two or more lines of systemic therapy. Epcoritamab is being co-developed by Genmab and AbbVie as part of the companies' oncology collaboration. The companies will share commercial responsibilities in the U.S. and Japan, with AbbVie responsible for further global commercialization. Genmab and AbbVie continue to evaluate the potential of epcoritamab, with ongoing clinical programs evaluating the therapy as a monotherapy and in combination regimens across treatment lines and a broad range of hematologic malignancies. Data from EPCORE DLBCL-2, evaluating fixed duration epcoritamab in combination with standard-of-care rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin hydrochloride, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP), in patients with newly diagnosed DLBCL are anticipated in 2026. This follows the recent disclosure of topline results from the Phase 3 EPCORE DLBCL-4 study, evaluating fixed-duration epcoritamab in a chemotherapy-free combination with lenalidomide in patients with R/R DLBCL. Epcoritamab is an IgG1-bispecific antibody created using Genmab's proprietary DuoBody® technology and administered subcutaneously. Genmab's DuoBody-CD3 technology is designed to direct cytotoxic T cells selectively to elicit an immune response toward target cell types. Epcoritamab is designed to simultaneously bind to CD3 on T cells and CD20 on B cells and induces T-cell-mediated killing of CD20+ cells.i Epcoritamab (approved under the brand name EPKINLY® in the U.S. and Japan, and TEPKINLY® in the EU) has received regulatory approval in certain lymphoma indications in more than 65 territories. Where approved, epcoritamab is a readily accessible therapy. Please see local country prescribing information for all labeled indication and safety information. About the EPCORE DLBCL-1 Trial EPCORE DLBCL-1 ( NCT04628494 ) is a global Phase 3 open label, multi-center, randomized trial to evaluate the efficacy of epcoritamab (GEN3013, DuoBody®-CD3xCD20) compared to investigator's choice of chemotherapy, either rituximab plus gemcitabine plus oxaliplatin (R-GemOx), or bendamustine plus rituximab (BR), in patients with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are ineligible for high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplant (HDT-ASCT). The trial started on January 13, 2021, and is ongoing. More information on this trial can be found at https://www.clinicaltrials.gov/ . About Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) worldwide, accounting for approximately 25-30 percent of all NHL cases.ii,iii In the U.S., there are approximately 25,000 new cases of DLBCL diagnosed each year.iv DLBCL can arise in lymph nodes as well as in organs outside of the lymphatic system, occurs more commonly in the elderly and is slightly more prevalent in men.v,vi DLBCL is a fast-growing type of NHL, a cancer that develops in the lymphatic system and affects B-cell lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. For many people living with DLBCL, their cancer either relapses, which means it may return after treatment, or becomes refractory, meaning it does not respond to treatment. Although new therapies have become available, treatment management can remain a challenge.iv,vii About Genmab Genmab is an international biotechnology company dedicated to improving the lives of people with cancer and other serious diseases through innovative antibody medicines. For over 25 years, its passionate, innovative and collaborative team has advanced a broad range of antibody-based therapeutic formats, including bispecific antibodies, antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs), immune-modulating antibodies and other next-generation modalities. Genmab’s science powers eight approved antibody medicines, and the company is advancing a strong late-stage clinical pipeline, including wholly owned programs, with the goal of delivering transformative medicines to patients. Established in 1999, Genmab is headquartered in Copenhagen, Denmark, with international presence across North America, Europe and Asia Pacific. For more information, please visit Genmab.com and follow us on LinkedIn and X . About AbbVie in Oncology AbbVie is committed to elevating standards of care and bringing transformative therapies to patients worldwide living with difficult-to-treat cancers. We are advancing a dynamic pipeline of investigational therapies across a range of cancer types in both blood cancers and solid tumors. We are focusing on creating targeted medicines that either impede the reproduction of cancer cells or enable their elimination. We achieve this through various, targeted treatment modalities and biology interventions, including small molecule therapeutics, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), immuno-oncology-based therapeutics, multispecific antibody and novel CAR-T platforms. Our dedicated and experienced team joins forces with innovative partners to accelerate the delivery of potential breakthrough medicines. Today, our expansive oncology portfolio is comprised of approved and investigational treatments for a wide range of blood and solid tumors. We are evaluating more than 35 investigational medicines across some of the world's most widespread and debilitating cancers. As we work to have a remarkable impact on people's lives, we are committed to exploring solutions to help patients obtain access to our cancer medicines. For more information, please visit us at http://www.abbvie.com/oncology .
